feedback: If the learner chops instead of rounding (e.g. 3.4567 to 2 dp written as 3.45), have them look at the digit just past the cut: 6 ≥ 5 means 3.4567 is past the midpoint 3.455 and so is nearer 3.46. Place it between 3.45 and 3.46 to see which is closer. (To 1 dp, chopping would give 3.4, but the correct answer is 3.5.)

If they round digit-by-digit (double rounding), use 3.4547 to 2 dp to show why it fails: rounding to 3 dp first gives 3.455, which then rounds up to 3.46, but a single decision at the hundredths place (decider thousandths 4 < 5) gives 3.45. Double rounding changed the answer — compare the full number to the single midpoint for the target place.
When a carry crosses a 9 (3.798 → 3.80), confirm the trailing zero stays because '2 decimal places' means two digits after the point.
If they are unsure about the exact-midpoint case, reinforce that at the midpoint and beyond the number rounds up to the higher candidate.
activities.intendedInsight: The midpoint IS the '5-and-above' rule: a number at or past halfway rounds up to the higher candidate. Rounding is one decision made at the target place by comparing nearness, not a digit-by-digit chop — and chopping or double rounding can give a different, wrong answer.
learnerActions: Pick a target precision (e.g. 1 decimal place) and draw a number line showing the two candidate values the number sits between — for 3.4567 to 1 dp, that is 3.4 and 3.5.
Mark the midpoint of the segment (3.45) clearly.
Place the number on the line (3.4567 lands just past the midpoint) and state which candidate it is nearer to.
State the rounded result (3.5) and point to the digit that decided it (the hundredths digit, 5, sits at/past halfway).
Repeat in whole-number mode: bracket 7,654,321 between 7,600,000 and 7,700,000, mark the midpoint 7,650,000, place the number, and round to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000).
Try a round-up cascade: place 3.798 to round to 2 dp between 3.79 and 3.80, see it is nearer 3.80, and write the trailing zero.

Compare two routes for rounding 3.4547 to 2 dp: round straight to 2 dp (decider is the thousandths 4, so 3.45) and also round to 3 dp first (3.455) then to 2 dp (3.46). Notice the answers differ — so make one decision at the target place, not a chain of roundings.
activities.title: Rounding as a nearness decision on a number line

feedback: If the learner gives 3.5 when 2 dp is asked, have them count decimal digits: 2 dp needs two, so the answer is 3.46.
If the wrong place is read for a large number, re-anchor on the chart: find the hundred-thousands column, then look one column to its right (the ten-thousands digit decides).
Keep the focus on the single decider digit, not on re-rounding digits further along.
activities.intendedInsight: Only the digit one place beyond the required accuracy decides the rounding; naming the target place prevents rounding to the wrong precision.
learnerActions: Write the number in a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
Circle the place you must round to and underline the single digit immediately beyond it — the decider.
Round 3.4567 to 2 dp (3.46) and say which digit decided it (the 6 in the thousandths).
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000) and name the deciding digit (the ten-thousands digit, 5).
Count the digits after the point aloud to confirm you gave the asked-for precision (e.g. 2 dp means exactly two decimal digits).
activities.title: Isolating the deciding digit with a place-value chart

feedback: If the learner writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, point out it now shows only one decimal place; the correct answer is 2.40.
Distinguish this from a rounding mistake — the rounding was right, only the recorded precision is missing the zero.
For 9.96 → 10.0, confirm the whole-number carry still leaves a tenths place that must read 0.
activities.intendedInsight: A rounded answer must display the required place even when a carry produces a zero there; the trailing zero records the precision, so dropping it changes what the answer claims.
learnerActions: Round 2.397 to 2 dp. The hundredths carry gives 2.40 — write the final 0.
Explain why 2.4 would be wrong for '2 decimal places' even though the value looks the same.
Round 9.96 to 1 dp (10.0) and keep the tenths zero.
Check each answer by counting that it shows exactly the required number of decimal places.
activities.title: Keeping placeholder zeros after a carry

feedback: If the estimate is far from the exact answer, check whether each factor was rounded to a sensible place.
Encourage stating the chosen rounding place so the estimate's accuracy can be judged.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding has a purpose beyond drill: it gives quick, sensible estimates to check whether an exact calculation is plausible.
learnerActions: Round each factor of 4.83 × 2.17 to a convenient value (5 × 2) and compute the estimate (10).
Compare your estimate to the exact product once calculated (≈ 10.48) and say whether the estimate is reasonable.
Try estimating another product or sum by rounding each number first, and state which place you rounded to and why.
activities.title: Rounding to estimate a calculation
